claims.text: An ML-augmented electronic-structure model that explicitly incorporates oxygen-induced defect scattering can accurately predict electrical conductivity of bulk HfNbTaTiZr over 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
Standard analytical conductivity predictions for HfNbTaTiZr assume perfect, defect-free crystals.
Bulk HfNbTaTiZr can be considered in both a nominally pure defect-free state and a state containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
First-principles CPA or ML-assisted defect-scattering calculations can represent local oxygen-induced disruptions of the electronic structure in HfNbTaTiZr.
Quantum and defect-scattering effects dominate electrical conductivity in HfNbTaTiZr over 0–200 K.
Thermal activation and phonon scattering play significant roles in HfNbTaTiZr conductivity over 300–1200 K.
Electrical-conductivity measurements in both stated temperature regimes are available for HfNbTaTiZr containing 1 wt.% oxygen.
Oxygen forms local interstitial defects in HfNbTaTiZr.
Oxygen defects act as electron-scattering centers that perturb the alloy's electronic band structure and conduction pathways.
Oxygen contamination induces localized electronic states and enhances electron scattering in HfNbTaTiZr.
At 0–200 K, oxygen-defect scattering lowers conductivity relative to perfect-crystal predictions.
At 300–1200 K, thermal effects partly overcome oxygen-defect scattering while conductivity remains modified.
The ML-augmented model can account for oxygen by adjusting electron relaxation times and energy-dependent scattering rates.
The model will reproduce a moderated conductivity decline or activation behavior over 300–1200 K.
The model will match conductivity data for 1 wt.% oxygen samples more accurately than methods that ignore defects.
Defect-free analytical approaches tend to overestimate conductivity and particularly fail at low temperatures.
The expected applicability is limited to bulk HfNbTaTiZr near 1 wt.% oxygen and the intervals 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
A conductivity prediction error greater than approximately 10% in either temperature regime would falsify the hypothesis.
Failure to reproduce lower low-temperature conductivity from oxygen defects relative to a perfect-crystal prediction would falsify the hypothesis.
